prompt_text: Explain how CRISPR gene editing works at a molecular level. Address the following: (1) the mechanism of target DNA recognition, (2) how the cut is made and repaired, (3) what can go wrong (off-target effects), and (4) the current limitations preventing widespread human germline editing.

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on vast text corpora to predict the next token in a sequence, thereby learning statistical patterns of language, reasoning, and world knowledge. Architecturally, modern LLMs are typically transformer-based, using self-attention mechanisms that allow the model to weigh the relevance of different words in a context window when generating each new token.

Training occurs in two main phases. Pre-training involves next-token prediction on billions or trillions of tokens, developing broad capabilities. Fine-tuning then aligns the model with specific tasks or human preferences, often using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or direct preference optimization (DPO).

The primary limitation is that LLMs do not possess genuine understanding or consciousness; they approximate reasoning through pattern matching and interpolation. They can hallucinate—generate plausible but false information—because they optimize for coherence rather than truth. Context windows, though expanding, remain finite, and reasoning degrades on tasks requiring many precise steps. Additionally, training data biases can propagate into outputs, and the models lack real-time access to information unless augmented with retrieval systems.
